comments.author: danpalmer
comments.text:
I'm really enjoying Order of the Sinking Star, but I'm in two minds about the length. It is long, I'm 20 hours in and still feel like I'm scratching the surface, and any story pay-off feels a very long way away, which isn't a great motivator.
However, so far I can't point to anything substantial that should have been skipped. Almost every level is teaching me something, and those things keep coming up later.
Ultimately, Order of the Sinking Star applies the same formula as The Witness (although hopefully with a little more story, but probably not a lot more), and dials it up to 11. I loved The Witness, so really it's exactly what I asked for, and I think the feeling of the distance left to go is an artifact of a desire for instant gratification.
I think the game is deeply rewarding and fantastic, as long as you understand you're signing up for a slow burn. That's not for everyone, and that's ok.

Context: BIPM is responsible for the UTC time standard, and in this document they decide to stop adding (or removing) leap seconds, starting on 20th of May 2027 and lasting for the foreseeable future (until one leap

is needed, but even then it's unclear if they'll do something). Together with the decision to not add a leap second in December, the 27 leap seconds that have been added so far should be the only ones, ever.

- It's a common source of bugs.

Negative
leap seconds have never occurred before, but might occur in the future, and almost no software has tested this case.
I'd also add:
- Unix timestamps are actually defined as "seconds since epoch
minus however many leap seconds have happened
". It's a hack to keep code that assumes "86400 seconds in a day" from breaking. It means that during a leap second the Unix timestamp goes back and repeats a previous value, making them ambiguous and non-monotonic.

comments.author: obviouslynotme
comments.text:
I used to work on software that still uses Fortran from the 50's and is still in maintenance and use today. IIRC, it had ~700kloc of Fortran. It may be the oldest and largest Fortran codebase still in use.
My first project there was removing all of the Hollerith from the code. Since Fortran predated strings, you had to manipulate them as integers. When you tied that to the original Fortran dynamic memory system, Dynosour, which used equivalenced arrays as pointers, it was a disaster.
It also gave me an appreciation for JavaBeanFactoryFactory. The original Fortran limited identifiers to six characters, the first of which indicated whether the variable was an integer, logical (bool), or real (float). I will take a 100 character name over ILBNK1 every single time.
GOTOs were surprisingly not a big problem, but structured code is definitely a bit easier to read, especially since it brought the practice of indentation with it.
Overall, it was a great experience but I wouldn't want to do it again, even if the work was interesting.

comments.author: whartung
comments.text:
FORTRAN was a very important language for me.
Growing up on early micros, with BASIC, my father had Fortran for the TRS-80.
I took a stab at learning it, but the documentation was reference for calling the compiler, not so much learning the language. And when I found a FORTRAN book, it was quite dated and talking about things like tapes and punches and what not.
So, that effort stalled.
But, my first quarter in college, I took a FORTRAN (77) class. FORTRAN taught on the schools CDC Cyber mainframe.
This was quite a change from 8-bit PET BASIC.
But, most importantly, it was exposure to much of the same concept that an 8-bit computer has, but from a different tact.
This gave me more of a way to view things from a higher level, since I had to make them fit the two different views of how FORTRAN looked at things, how the Cyber presented things, and how BASIC and the PET were "same thing only different".
It also gave me access to a multi-user system, and all of the interesting capabilities it offers.
I remember when they put in their first lab of PCs, and how they started teaching folks Turbo Pascal on micro computers, and I just felt that the users were missing out on a bigger world. "

As an example, to show off my LLM-reverse-engineered-hardware project: a user-space driver and software for an old FireWire to USB box, the manufacturer drivers for which were last updated in 2006 and don't really work anymore on modern OSes (and never worked on Mac). stories.title_en: Non-Determinism Doesn't Matter

comments.author: delifue
comments.text:
When people refute the idea that "LLM is the new compiler from natural language to code" the common reason is that LLM is non-deterministic but compiler is deterministic.
But the determinism isn't the real distinction. LLM inference can be made deterministic (temparaute zero, etc.). And multi-threaded compiler can be non-dterministic.
And human developers are also non-deterministic. There is always the nondeterminism even before AI.
I think the real difference is how leaky the abstraction is. If you just need to understand language instead of compiler internal to write correct code, the compiler is non-leaky abstrction. If you rely on compiler to do auto SIMD optimization, and have to do hacks to trigger the optimization, compiler is leaky abstraction.
For AI, if you don't ever need to read the code and AI writes perfectly bug-free program that perfectly follows instruction, then AI is a non-leaky abstraction, but that's not the case for now. To make code maintainable and debuggable you still need to read the code if the project is complex enough.

comments.author: Dwedit
comments.text:
Given the same text input, same hardware type (inference on CPU vs on GPU), and
same RNG seed
, you will get the same exact output.  That is deterministic.
That was from when I was testing out someone's claim that koboldcpp got less smart in a newer release, but I was reproducing the exact same output across different versions of the program.

comments.author: augment_me
comments.text:
Orthogonal to the blog, but fun fact: Determinism is crucial for large-scale training runs, and effective RL-runs as it avoids collapse of numerics, but it costs more(about 20% perf) because you need can't parallelize over the batch nor use some specific instructions that dont guarantee reduction order in the way way. Horace He from Thinky has a great blog about this:
https://thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in...

comments.author: emtel
comments.text:
This debate conflates two senses of the word deterministic:
1. Repeatable: the same inputs always lead to the same outputs
2. Algorithmic: the answer is arrived at by a set of steps that can clearly be shown to produce output with some desired property.
(2 is not a textbook definition of deterministic that I’ve ever heard, but I think it’s what people mean here)
LLMs don’t usually satisfy definition 1. They could, in principle, but it wouldn’t matter if they did. It wouldn’t tell you anything about whether the outputs are trustworthy.
What people seem to want is 2, but 2 is, I think, a contradiction. There cannot be an algorithmic process that can turns a natural language prompt into a working program, because natural language is too ambiguous to specify an output.
Nevertheless I agree with the main point of the article. Non-algorithmic processes (like intelligence) can produce algorithmic processes (like software). After all that’s what human programmers do!

comments.author: Marha01
comments.text: The important factor is not determinism vs. non-determinism, that is just an implementation detail. The important factor is simply the rate of mistakes or bugs the LLM makes. If it is low enough, the problem is for all practical purposes gone. Is it low enough today, or not? That is the question..

The problem isn't non determinism, but that changing a single token in the input can change the output completely. And you can't put that somewhere in production completely unattended.
It's the uncertainty of "who knows what the machine will output this time" if you have no idea of what the input is going to be.

I hope that we will soon see deterministic inference offered by frontier labs (presumably at a premium rate). In the meantime, you can get deterministic behavior from local models using the right vLLM flags. I've described some of the cool applications of determinism here:
